subtype: Approach: following a friend's tip on a hot stock [Pitfall]
passage:
Monday
Charu: Have you seen that stock? It's beaten down. It'll double, I'm sure of it.
Payal: How sure?
Charu: Very. Someone at lunch said so. Don't wait too long.
Payal: I don't have time to read up. But okay, I'll put in a big chunk 🙂
Three weeks later
Payal: The stock is down again. Just read the annual report. It has huge debts, and interest payments eat everything.
Charu: Oh no. I only heard it from someone else. I'm so sorry 😢
Payal: I'm not blaming you. I should have looked before.
Charu: What will you do now?
Payal: Read properly. And talk to someone qualified before I put anything else in.

qa.q: What did Payal read three weeks later?
What was Payal feeling by the end of the chat?
qa.a: Payal was regretful and worried, but calm and clear enough to accept responsibility for not looking first.

qa.q: What could Payal do before putting money into another stock?
qa.a: Payal could read the company's reports first and talk with a qualified adviser about how much risk fits.

qa.q: How might Charu have felt on hearing about the debts?
qa.a: Charu felt guilty and embarrassed about passing on a tip heard second-hand, as the sorry message shows.

grounding: The chat shows an investor putting a large sum into a beaten-down stock on a colleague's claim, without research, and later finding serious debt.

subtype: Approach: following a friend's tip on a hot stock [Pitfall]
passage:
At the co-operative bank branch in the small town of Karad, Rafiq leaned over Aadhya's desk at lunch. "Listen. That cement company's share has fallen sixty percent. My cousin in Mumbai says it will double by Diwali. Put something in now, before everyone else does."
Aadhya had ₹1.5 lakh saved for her sister's wedding. Rafiq sounded so sure. That evening, without reading anything about the company, she put in a lakh.
For two weeks the price went up a little, and she felt clever. Then it fell. And fell. In December the newspaper said the company had defaulted on its loans; it owed far more than it could pay, and had for months. The share was worth almost nothing.
Rafiq avoided her in the canteen. Aadhya sat on the bus home doing the maths again and again, wondering how to tell her mother about the wedding money.

qa.q: How much did Aadhya put in?
qa.a: A lakh, out of the ₹1.5 lakh saved.

qa.q: How did Aadhya feel on the bus home?
qa.a: Aadhya felt sick with worry and guilt, dreading telling her mother about the wedding money.

qa.q: What could Aadhya have done before investing?
qa.a: Read about the company's debts, kept money meant for a near-term need out of it, and asked a qualified adviser instead of acting on a tip.

qa.q: Why might Rafiq avoid Aadhya in the canteen?
qa.a: Rafiq probably feels embarrassed and guilty that his confident tip cost her so much.

grounding: It shows a young woman putting a large sum into a beaten-down stock on a colleague's tip without research, then learning the company had serious debt problems.

subtype: Approach: following a friend's tip on a hot stock [Pitfall]
passage:
Esther was certain. "It's down seventy percent, Ingrid. Everyone's panicking, which means it's the bottom. My brother-in-law works in finance and says it'll double within a year." She meant a furniture retailer whose name had been all over the news in Oslo.
Ingrid had been saving for a flat deposit. She didn't read the company's reports; they looked long and dull. She moved half her savings into the stock the next morning and texted Esther a thumbs-up.
Three months later the company announced it couldn't pay its lenders. It had been carrying huge debts for years; the fall had been a warning, not a bargain. Trading in the shares was stopped. Ingrid's flat deposit was now a fraction of what it had been.
That night she read the reports properly for the first time. The debt was right there, on page four.

qa.q: Where in the reports was the debt shown?
How did Ingrid feel reading the reports that night?
qa.a: Ingrid likely felt foolish and sick, seeing that the warning had been there all along.

qa.q: What could Ingrid have done differently?
qa.a: Read the reports before investing, kept her flat-deposit money out of a single risky stock, and asked a qualified adviser.

qa.q: How might Esther feel after trading in the shares was stopped?
qa.a: Esther may feel guilty and embarrassed that her confident tip helped cost Ingrid so much.

grounding: It shows a young woman investing a large part of her savings in a fallen stock on a colleague's tip without research, then finding the company had deep debt problems.
